title: Streams, Redirection & Pipes
sub: How commands pass data to each other, and how you wire them together
goals: Explain stdin, stdout and stderr and redirect each one on its own
Chain commands with pipes and read a pipeline from left to right
Feed one command's output into another command's arguments with $(), xargs and <()
Use exit codes, &&, || and pipefail so chains fail safely
Build a five-stage pipeline from scratch against real log data

blocks.text: Every program you start in a terminal is wired to three channels: it reads from one and writes to two. Apart from launching programs, the shell's main job is deciding where those channels point. Once you can re-wire them, small single-purpose tools snap together into something that answers a question nobody wrote a program for. That is the idea behind pipes, and it is the most valuable skill in this book to practice until it is automatic.

Open Terminal and create the practice lab with the **Lab Kit** in [Setting up your lab](#setup). Every example below that mentions `access.log`, `ips.txt` or `users.csv` uses those files, so your results will match the ones printed here. Type the commands instead of pasting them whenever you can; your fingers learn syntax your eyes only recognize.
The three standard streams

A **stream** is an ordered flow of bytes. When the kernel starts a process it hands it three open streams, each identified by a small integer called a **file descriptor** (fd). Programs do not know or care what is on the other end: a terminal, a file, a network socket or another program.

blocks.code:
┌──────────────────────────────┐
  keyboard ──────▶ │ fd 0   stdin                 │
  file, or pipe    │                              │
                   │          P R O C E S S       │ ──▶ fd 1  stdout ──▶ terminal, file or next command
                   │        (ls, grep, ping...)   │ ──▶ fd 2  stderr ──▶ terminal or file
                   └──────────────────────────────┘

blocks.text: Both output streams end up on your screen, so they look identical. They are separate channels on purpose: you can save or pipe the *results* while the *error messages* still reach you.

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ ls README.txt nothing.txt > out.txt
ls: nothing.txt: No such file or directory
$ cat out.txt
README.txt

blocks.text: The error appeared on screen even though `>` captured the output. `out.txt` holds only the listing, because `>` redirects fd 1 and the complaint travelled on fd 2.

Unix tools do one thing, read text lines from stdin and write text lines to stdout, and let the shell do the connecting. Any tool that follows that contract can be combined with any other, including ones written decades apart. That is why `grep` (1973) happily filters the output of `curl` (1996) or a Python script you wrote this morning.
Redirection: pointing a stream somewhere else
Redirection is performed by the shell *before* the program starts. The program simply writes to "stdout"; it never sees the file.

head: Operator
Meaning
Example
rows: stdout to a file, replacing its contents
stdout appended to the end of a file
stderr to wherever stdout points right now
stdout and stderr to a file (zsh and bash)

blocks.text: `/dev/null` is a special file that accepts any amount of data and throws it away. It is how you silence a stream.

blocks.title: Capture everything a command prints into one file

tokens.exp: flag: stop after 3 probes, then print statistics
redirect stdout (fd 1) into a file, truncating it first
make fd 2 (stderr) point at wherever fd 1 points at this moment

blocks.text: Order matters
The shell processes redirections strictly left to right, and `2>&1` means "copy where fd 1 points *now*". Compare:

blocks.code:
ping -c1 nohost.invalid > all.txt 2>&1          ping -c1 nohost.invalid 2>&1 > all.txt

 1. fd1 ──▶ all.txt                              1. fd2 ──▶ terminal   (fd1 still points there)
 2. fd2 ──▶ same place as fd1 = all.txt          2. fd1 ──▶ all.txt
 result: both streams in the file  ✔             result: error still prints on screen  ✘

blocks.text: Read it as two assignments: `>` sets fd 1, then `2>&1` copies fd 1 into fd 2. Swap them and fd 2 copies the old destination.

items.text: `&>` and `&>>` work in zsh exactly as in bash. `cmd >& file` is the older csh spelling and also works.

zsh has a **MULTIOS** feature, on by default: `echo hi > a.txt > b.txt` writes to *both* files, and `cat < a.txt < b.txt` reads both in turn. Bash does not do this, so avoid depending on it in scripts you share.
`setopt NO_CLOBBER` makes `>` refuse to overwrite an existing file (use `>|` to force it). Handy while learning; add it to `~/.zshrc` if you like the safety net.

blocks.sum: Redirect a command's standard output into a file, replacing whatever the file held.

how.text: The shell opens `file` for writing before the command starts, creating it or truncating it to zero bytes, and points fd 1 at it. Because the truncation happens first, `sort data.txt > data.txt` empties the file before `sort` reads a single line. Write to a new file, then `mv` it over the original.
Only stdout is captured. Anything the program prints to stderr still reaches the terminal unless you also redirect fd 2.

examples.desc: Save a long listing to a file
Create an empty file, or empty an existing one
Show the five biggest files on screen and keep a copy

gotchas: `>` overwrites without asking. `setopt NO_CLOBBER` in zsh turns that into an error; `>|` overrides the protection for one command.

blocks.sum: Append a command's standard output to the end of a file, creating it if needed.

how.text: Same as `>` but the file is opened in append mode: existing contents stay, and every write lands at the current end of the file. This makes `>>` the right tool for logs and for building a file one command at a time.

examples.desc: Add a timestamped line to a log
Append only the failed requests from today's log to an archive

blocks.sum: Feed a file to a command's standard input.

how.text: The shell opens `file` for reading and points fd 0 at it, so the command behaves as if you had typed the file's contents. Many tools accept a filename argument instead (`sort ips.txt`), but `<` works for programs that only read stdin, and it keeps the filename out of the output: `wc -l < ips.txt` prints just a number, while `wc -l ips.txt` also prints the name.

examples.desc: Count lines without the file name
Sort a file and keep only unique lines

blocks.sum: Point stderr at wherever stdout currently points, so both streams travel together.

how.text: `n>&m` duplicates file descriptor `m` onto `n`. With `2>&1`, fd 2 becomes a copy of fd 1 *as it is at that moment*, which is why it must come after `> file`. Without a file redirection it merges stderr into the pipe, so the next command sees errors too. zsh and bash also offer `|&` as shorthand for `2>&1 |`, and `&>` for `> file 2>&1`.

examples.desc: Log everything a script prints
Same thing with the shorthand
Search errors and normal output together

gotchas: `cmd 2>&1 > file` does not do what it looks like: stderr is copied to the old stdout (the terminal) before stdout moves to the file.

blocks.text: Pipes: connecting stdout to stdin
A pipe connects the stdout of one process directly to the stdin of the next. Nothing is written to disk. The kernel holds a small in-memory buffer (typically 16 to 64 KB) between the two processes.
Three facts explain almost every surprise you will meet:

items.text: **All stages start at once.** `cat | grep | wc` launches three processes simultaneously. Data flows through as it is produced, so `head` can stop a huge job early: once `head` has its lines it exits, the upstream program gets a "broken pipe" signal and stops too.
**The buffer applies back-pressure.** If the consumer is slow, the producer blocks when the buffer is full. A pipeline never uses more memory than one buffer per join, however large the data.
**Only stdout goes through.** Errors from any stage still print on your terminal, which is usually what you want. To send them down the pipe as well, use `2>&1 |` or zsh's `|&`.

blocks.text: Reading a pipeline
Read left to right and ask of each `|`: *what shape is the data on this side?* A pipeline is a series of transformations, and you can inspect the data after any stage by cutting the pipeline there.
Each line gets a little smaller and more focused. That is the working method: **build it one stage at a time, run it after every `|`, and only add the next stage when the output looks right.**
The toolbox you pipe through
Nearly every pipeline is made of a few kinds of stages. Chapter [Text-processing toolkit](#text) covers each tool in depth; this table is the map.

head: Role
Tools
What it does to the stream
rows: creates the first lines of data
keeps some lines, drops the rest
merges repeated lines, optionally counting them
turns many lines into one number
copies the stream to a file and passes it on
turns output into arguments or into a file

blocks.text: The five-stage recipe
Most "how many / which / how often" questions about log data fit one shape: **produce → filter → extract → count → rank.**

blocks.code:
$ cd ~/lab
$ grep -c ' 404 ' access.log
11
$ grep ' 404 ' access.log | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3
   4 /wp-login.php
   3 /api/v1/users
   3 /admin

blocks.text: Read the second command aloud: *find the 404 lines, take the requested path (field 7), sort so identical paths touch, count each run of identical paths, rank by count descending, keep the top three.* The first `sort` exists only to make `uniq` work, because `uniq` merges **adjacent** duplicates.

`uniq` compares each line with the previous one. Without a `sort` in front, `a b a` stays `a b a`. If you see duplicate lines after `uniq`, you forgot to sort. `sort -u` does both jobs in one step when you do not need the counts.
Why the leading spaces?

On macOS, `uniq -c` and `wc` right-align their numbers with leading spaces. That is harmless to read but can break string comparisons: `[[ $(wc -l < f) == 10 ]]` is false when the output is `      10`, while the arithmetic test `-eq 10` tolerates the spaces. Strip them with `tr -d ' '`, or let `awk` reprint the field: `awk '{print $1}'`.
Output as input: three ways to hand data over

A pipe only works when the next program *reads stdin*. Plenty of commands want their data as **arguments** (`ls -l FILE...`, `kill PID...`, `rm FILE...`) or as a **file** (`diff A B`). Shells give you three adapters:

blocks.name: xargs
blocks.sum: Read items from stdin and run another command with those items as its arguments.

how.text: `xargs` is the adapter between "lines on stdin" and "arguments on a command line". It splits its input on whitespace (or newlines, with `-I`, or NUL bytes, with `-0`), then calls `command` with as many items as fit. With no command it runs `echo`.

Three modes cover nearly all use: batch mode (default, many items per call), one-at-a-time (`-n 1`), and placeholder mode (`-I {}`, where each input line replaces `{}` in the command, one call per line).

flags.d: Use at most N arguments per command invocation (`-n 1` runs the command once per item).
Replace every `{}` in the command with each input line; implies one line per call.
Input items are separated by NUL bytes, not whitespace. Pair it with `find -print0` so names with spaces survive.
Run up to N commands in parallel. Output from parallel jobs can interleave.
Print each command to stderr before running it. Great for debugging a pipeline.
Ask for confirmation before each command.

examples.desc: Ping each host in a list once
Delete every .tmp file under a folder, safely handling spaces in names
Resolve every domain in hosts.txt and show the first IP for each
examples.code: cat hosts.txt | xargs -I {} sh -c 'printf "%s " {}; dig +short {} | head -1'

anat.exp: placeholder: each input line is substituted for {}
a shell to run the quoted script, so the pipe inside works per item
the command template; {} becomes the host name

gotchas: With empty input, macOS (BSD) `xargs` runs nothing, but GNU `xargs` on Linux runs the command once anyway unless you pass `-r`. Scripts meant for both should pass `-r`; macOS accepts it and ignores it.
Putting `{}` inside an `sh -c '...'` string splices the input text into shell code. Only do that with data you trust.
Names containing spaces or quotes split into several arguments unless you use `-0` with NUL-separated input.

blocks.sum: Replace the expression with the stdout of a command, then use that text as part of a bigger command.

how.text: The shell runs the inner command first, captures its stdout, strips trailing newlines and splices the result into the outer command line. Unquoted, the result is split into words on whitespace; quoted (`"$(...)"`), it stays one word. Backticks `` `cmd` `` do the same but nest badly; prefer `$( )`.

examples.desc: Put today's date in a file name
Store a result in a variable
Ping your gateway without looking up its address first

anat.exp: start command substitution: run what follows, paste its output here
prints routing details for the default route
keeps the line containing "gateway:" and prints its second field

gotchas: Quote it when the result may contain spaces: `ls -l "$(pwd)"`.

blocks.sum: Run a command and give its output to another command as if it were a file.

how.text: The shell runs the inner command in the background, connects its stdout to a pipe, and substitutes a path like `/dev/fd/11` for the whole expression. The outer command opens that "file" normally. This is the answer when a command needs *files* but your data is the output of other commands, as with `diff` or `comm`. zsh also has `=( )`, which writes to a real temporary file when the program needs a seekable file, and `>( )` for the output side.

examples.desc: Compare two commands' output
Which IPs appear in both files?
examples.code: comm -12 <(sort ips.txt | uniq) <(awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq)

gotchas: Plain `<( )` is not seekable; if a program complains it cannot rewind or seek, use zsh's `=( )` instead.

blocks.name: tee
blocks.sum: Copy stdin to stdout and to one or more files at the same time.

how.text: `tee` is a T-junction for a pipeline: it passes everything through unchanged while writing a copy to each named file. Use it to save an intermediate result without breaking the chain, or, with `sudo tee`, to write a root-owned file from a pipe, which `sudo cmd > file` cannot do because the redirection runs as *you*.

flags.d: Append to the files instead of truncating them.

examples.desc: Watch output and save it
Save the raw 404 lines and keep processing them
Write a root-owned file from a pipe

gotchas: `tee` truncates by default. Add `-a` to append to an existing file.

blocks.text: Exit codes and control operators

Every command finishes with an **exit status**: a number from 0 to 255 that the shell stores in `$?`. **Zero means success; anything else means failure.** The convention is older than the shell itself, and the control operators are built on it.

head: Operator
Name
Right side runs when...
rows: immediately; `a` keeps running in the background
groups commands in a child shell, so `cd` and variable changes do not leak out
groups commands in the current shell (needs the trailing `;` and the spaces)

blocks.text: Common statuses: `0` success, `1` general failure, `2` misuse of a command, `126` found but not executable, `127` command not found, `130` stopped with Ctrl-C (128 + signal 2).

blocks.code:
$ ls /nonexistent; echo "status was $?"
ls: /nonexistent: No such file or directory
status was 1
$ mkdir -p /tmp/demo && cd /tmp/demo && echo "now in $PWD"
now in /tmp/demo

blocks.title: a && b || c is not an if/else

blocks.text: `test -f {{file}} && echo yes || echo no` prints `no` when the file exists but `echo yes` itself fails (for example when stdout is closed). More importantly, `build && deploy || rollback` runs `rollback` when `deploy` fails, which may not be what you intended. For real branching use `if ...; then ...; else ...; fi`, covered in [Scripting](#scripting).
The status of a pipeline
By default a pipeline's exit status is the status of its **last** stage, so a failure early in the chain is invisible:

blocks.code:
$ false | true; echo $?
0
$ setopt pipefail
$ false | true; echo $?
1
$ false | true; echo $pipestatus
1 0

blocks.text: With `setopt pipefail` the status becomes that of the rightmost stage that failed. zsh's `pipestatus` array (bash calls it `PIPESTATUS`, upper-case) holds every stage's status for the most recent pipeline, so you can see *which* stage failed. Put `setopt pipefail` at the top of any script that uses pipes.

blocks.sum: Run the next command only if the previous one succeeded (&&) or failed (||).

how.text: `&&` and `||` look at the exit status of the command to their left. They group left to right with equal precedence, short-circuit like boolean operators, and are the shell's cheapest conditionals. They also make scripts safe: `cd build && make` will not run `make` in the wrong directory when `cd` fails.

examples.desc: Only continue if the directory was created
Fall back to a message when a check fails
Back up a file, then say so, but only if the copy worked

gotchas: `a && b || c` runs `c` when `a` fails *or* when `b` fails.

blocks.sum: Feed a block of literal text to a command's stdin (here-document), or a single string with <<<.

how.text: A **here-document** reads the lines that follow, up to a line containing only the delimiter, and sends them to stdin. Quote the delimiter (`<<'EOF'`) to stop the shell from expanding `$variables` and `$( )` inside the text. A **here-string** (`<<<`) sends one string plus a newline, which is a tidy way to run a command on a variable without `echo ... |`.

examples.desc: Write a small config file in one command
Run a command on a string
Count the words in a variable

gotchas: With plain `<<EOF` the shell still expands `$HOME` and backticks inside the body. Use `<<'EOF'` when the text must stay literal, such as when generating another script.

blocks.text: Practice
Work through these in your own Terminal, inside `~/lab`. Try the exercise before opening the hint, and open the hint before the solution. Being stuck for a minute is the part that builds skill.

blocks.title: Split the streams

task.text: Run one command that lists `README.txt` **and** `nothing.txt` (which does not exist), sending the listing to `good.txt` and the error message to `bad.txt`. Then check that each file holds what you expect.

hints: You need two redirections on one command: one for fd 1, one for fd 2.
blocks.solution:
ls README.txt nothing.txt > good.txt 2> bad.txt
cat good.txt
cat bad.txt

why.text: Redirections are independent and evaluated left to right. `> good.txt` rebinds fd 1 and `2> bad.txt` rebinds fd 2, so each stream goes to its own file.

blocks.verify: [[ -s good.txt && -s bad.txt ]] && echo "OK: both files have content"

blocks.title: Unique visitors

task.text: How many *different* client IP addresses appear in `access.log`? Use a pipeline that ends in a single number.

hints: The client IP is the first whitespace-separated field on each line.
`awk '{print $1}'` prints field 1. Something must remove duplicates before you count.

why.text: `awk` extracts, `sort -u` sorts and drops duplicates in one step, `wc -l` counts the survivors. `sort | uniq | wc -l` gives the same answer with one more process.

blocks.title: Top three talkers

task.text: Print the three client IPs that made the most requests, each preceded by its request count, biggest first.

hints: You need counts per IP, so think `uniq -c`, and `uniq` needs sorted input.
Sort the counts numerically in reverse (`sort -rn`) and keep the first three lines with `head`.
blocks.solution: awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -3

why.text: This is the classic *count-and-rank* idiom: `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`. You will reuse it for status codes, paths, user agents and ports in later chapters.

blocks.title: Silence the noise

task.text: Search your whole home folder for files whose name ends in `.log`, showing only the first 10 results and hiding every "Permission denied" message.

hints: The permission errors travel on stderr (fd 2).

why.text: `2> /dev/null` discards fd 2 before the pipe is set up, so only stdout flows into `head`. Without it, the errors would interleave with your results on screen.

blocks.title: Arguments from output

task.text: Show a long listing (`ls -l`) of only the three most recently modified entries in `~/lab`, in two different ways: once with `xargs`, once with `$( )`.

hints: `ls -t` sorts newest first. `head -3` keeps three names.
blocks.solution:
ls -t | head -3 | xargs ls -l
ls -l $(ls -t | head -3)

why.text: `xargs` turns the three lines into arguments of `ls -l`; `$( )` pastes the same three names directly into the command line. Both break on file names that contain spaces. `find -print0 | xargs -0` is the robust form.

blocks.title: Which stage failed?

task.text: Run a three-stage pipeline in which the *middle* command fails, then print the status of every stage on one line. Do it in a way that works in zsh.

hints: The command `false` always fails; `true` always succeeds.
zsh stores every stage's status in the `pipestatus` array.

why.text: `$?` reports only the last stage (0 here). `pipestatus` is a zsh array holding `0 1 0`, so the second stage is the culprit.

questions.q: Which operator captures only error messages in a file?
questions.why: stderr is file descriptor 2, so `2>` redirects it. `>` is shorthand for `1>` (stdout only).

options.text: Prints an error because the file is in use
Empties the file, because the shell truncates it before sort reads it

questions.why: The shell performs the redirection first, truncating `data.txt` to zero bytes. `sort` then reads an empty file.

questions.q: In `cmd 2>&1 > out.txt`, where does stderr go?
questions.why: `2>&1` copies where fd 1 points *at that moment*: the terminal. Only afterwards does `> out.txt` move fd 1.

questions.q: Which construct lets `diff` compare the sorted output of two commands without temporary files?
questions.why: Process substitution `<( )` presents each command's output as a file path that `diff` can open.

questions.q: Which `xargs` flag lets you place each input line anywhere in the command using `{}`?
questions.why: `-I {}` (any replacement string works) substitutes each line for the placeholder and runs the command once per line.

questions.q: A pipeline `false | true` reports status 0 in zsh. Which option makes it report the failure?
questions.why: `pipefail` makes the pipeline's status that of the rightmost command that failed. `pipestatus` shows every stage.

blocks.text: Build three one-liners that you could run against any web-server log, and save them as a reusable zsh script. You will turn the script into a proper tool in [Scripting](#scripting).
Step 1: Rank the clients
Write a pipeline that prints the top 5 client IPs with counts and saves the ranking to `top-ips.txt` while still showing it on screen.

blocks.code: awk '{print $1}' {{logfile}} | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5 | tee top-ips.txt

blocks.text: Step 2: Histogram of status codes
Count how many responses each HTTP status code (field 9) got, most common first.
Step 3: Suspicious probes

List every request path that returned 401, 403 or 404 and was fetched by an IP that appears more than 10 times in total. Think in two stages: first build the list of busy IPs, then use `grep -F -f` or `awk` to keep lines from those IPs.

blocks.code:
awk '{print $1}' {{logfile}} | sort | uniq -c | awk '$1 > 10 {print $2}' > busy.txt
grep -F -w -f busy.txt {{logfile}} | awk '$9 ~ /^(401|403|404)$/ {print $1, $7, $9}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

blocks.text: Step 4: Save it as a script
Put the three commands in `triage.zsh`, make it executable and run it with `./triage.zsh`.

blocks.code:
#!/bin/zsh
# Usage: ./triage.zsh access.log
setopt pipefail
log=${1:?usage: triage.zsh LOGFILE}
echo "== top clients =="
awk '{print $1}' "$log" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
echo "== status codes =="
awk '{print $9}' "$log" | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
